item.title: Honda plans highway test of wireless charging for moving trucks
item.description: Japanese automaker Honda Motor said on Monday it has developed technology that can wirelessly charge electric vehicles, including large trucks, while being driven, and plans to test the technology on a Japanese highway.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Japanese automaker Honda Motor (7267.T) said on Monday it has developed technology that can wirelessly charge electric vehicles, including large trucks, while being driven, and plans to test the technology on a Japanese highway. Honda plans to test the technology along with construction firm Taisei (1801.T) and road builder Taisei Rotec in the financial year beginning in April 2027 or later, it said in a statement The system, developed by Honda's research arm with the two firms, aims to transfer electricity wirelessly from charging units embedded in roads to vehicles in motion, which could lead to fewer charging stops A Honda engineer declined to comment on the cost compared with a conventional high-speed charging network, saying economic viability would need to be assessed

item.title: High-flying Penguins aim to keep pouring in goals against Jets
item.description: The high-scoring Pittsburgh Penguins look to continue their hot start when they host the Winnipeg Jets on Monday night.
item.dc:creator: Field Level Media
item.content:encoded: The high-scoring Pittsburgh Penguins look to continue their hot start when they host the Winnipeg Jets on Monday night. After winning their first two games by scores of 7-0 and 6-5 (in overtime), the Penguins will catch the Jets on the second half of a back-to-back. Winnipeg has split its first two games after a 3-2 road win over the Detroit Red Wings on Sunday. Kyle Connor had two goals and an assist and Stuart Skinner, signed as a free agent on July 1, made 33 saves to earn his first win for the Jets. Connor's second goal made it 3-0 early in the second period and Winnipeg held on thanks in large part to Connor's 56th career three-point game. Connor has three goals and two assists through two games. "Through two games, he has just been dominating with the puck," Jets coach Scott Arniel said of Connor. "But the play I remember is him tracking back to break up a 3-on-2. He does those things on both ends of the ice." Cole Perfetti had a goal and two assists for the Jets, who were 3-for-4 on the power play while holding the Red Wings to a 1-for-5 effort. "I think it is safe to say our special teams played a huge role in that win," Perfetti said. "The power play got three early in the game, and then the penalty kill did a great job late before they killed the 6-on-5 at the end." The Penguins are showing strong special teams play of their own, going 4-for-8 on the power play through two games while their opponents are 0-for-5. On Saturday against the visiting Montreal Canadians, Pittsburgh squandered a four-goal lead but Tommy Novak's second goal of the game, coming 1:33 into overtime, gave the Penguins the 6-5 win. Evgeni Malkin had a goal and two assists, and Arturs Silovs made 20 saves. Erik Karlsson and Kris Letang each had two assists, and Novak added one. The Penguins led by 5-2 after two periods, but the Canadiens scored three straight goals, including two in the final 1:08 of the third period, to force overtime. "We found a way," Penguins coach Dan Muse said. "We got the two points. We got plenty that we can look at now that we know we got to fix, and I'm confident that this group will work to correct those things. Forward Ben Kindel, who missed the opener due to a lower-body injury, scored on a power play in his season debut. "Some good, some bad," said Kindel. "Obviously, the first game coming back here, I felt like it kind of took a little bit to get going. Started making some plays but still some stuff to work on as well." Malkin has goals in each of the first two games, becoming the second 40-year-old in NHL history to do so, joining Gordie Howe (1968-69). Sidney Crosby, 39, has an assist in each of Pittsburgh's two games. Last season, the Jets and Penguins split a pair of games. On Nov. 1, Connor had two goals and the Jets won 5-2 in Winnipeg. The Penguins prevailed 5-4 at home in a shootout on March 21. Karlsson scored twice and Rickard Rakell had the shootout winner. --Field Level Media

item.content:encoded: Trotz besserer Konjunkturlage hat sich die Stimmung unter den deutschen Verbrauchern wenige Wochen vor dem beginnenden Weihnachtsgeschäft eingetrübt. Das Barometer für das Konsumklima sank im Oktober um 1,19 Punkte auf 93,51 Zähler, wie der Handelsverband Deutschland (HDE) am Montag zu seiner Umfrage unter 1600 Verbrauchern mitteilte. Es liegt damit auch deutlich unter dem Niveau des Vorjahresmonats. "Eine Belebung des privaten Konsums zeigt sich aktuell nicht – trotz der Verbesserung der gesamtwirtschaftlichen Entwicklung", lautet das Fazit des HDE. "Damit trüben sich auch die Erwartungen für das Weihnachtsgeschäft etwas ein." Am Jahresende fahren viele Geschäfte einen großen Teil ihres Umsatzes ein. Besonders die negative Entwicklung der Anschaffungsneigung der Verbraucher dämpft die Aussichten. Der aktuelle Wert liegt deutlich unter dem Vorjahreswert. Auch die Einkommenserwartungen haben sich spürbar verschlechtert. "Immerhin positiv ist der Blick auf die Sparneigung", hieß es. Die Befragten planen demnach für die kommenden Wochen, ihre Sparneigung nicht weiter zu erhöhen. Auch die Konjunkturerwartungen sinken zum Vormonat - und das, obwohl führende Wirtschaftsforschungsinstitute ihre Wachstumsprognose für Europas größte Volkswirtschaft in diesem Jahr auf 1,3 Prozent mehr als verdoppelt haben. Die Verbraucher gehen allerdings von einem Rückgang ihres verfügbaren Einkommens aus. "Die zuletzt gestiegenen Energiepreise sowie die hohen Spritpreise belasten die Konsumenten und hemmen die Konsumstimmung", betonte der HDE. Die Verbraucher erwarten zudem eine steigende Inflationsrate. Rekordhohe Spritpreise haben die Inflation in Deutschland im September auf den höchsten Stand seit fast drei Jahren getrieben. Waren und Dienstleistungen verteuerten sich um 3,3 Prozent zum Vorjahresmonat, nach 2,9 Prozent im August. Einen höheren Wert gab es zuletzt im Dezember 2023 mit 3,7 Prozent. Seit dem 1. Oktober bis zum Jahresende gilt ein neuer Tankrabatt - eine Subvention, die bereits im Mai und Juni zum Tragen kam und die Inflation etwas dämpfen könnte.

item.title: Spanish PM Sanchez to make morning announcement amid speculation about early election
item.description: Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez will make an institutional declaration at 9 a.m. local time (0700 GMT) on Monday, his office said, amid widespread expectations he will call an early general election.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez will make an institutional declaration at 9 a.m. local time (0700 GMT) on Monday, his office said, amid widespread expectations he will call an early general election. The potential decision to move the election forward despite it being scheduled for next year would come after the lower house of parliament on Friday rejected the government's attempt to curb the country's housing crisis amid massive protests. "It's logical to call elections now. There will not be a more favourable scenario. It's risky and he could lose the government but nonetheless, I don't think that he will have a better moment," said political analyst Eduardo Bayon. However, Sanchez has repeatedly insisted the elections would be in 2027 and that he would finish the constitutional four-year term. A government spokesperson declined to confirm the nature of the announcement ahead of time.

item.description: Lidl GB, the UK arm of the German discounter, said on Monday it would open over 50 new stores in its current financial year as part of a £600 million ($793 million) investment, seeking a bigger slice of Britain's grocery market.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Lidl GB, the UK arm of the German discounter, said on Monday it would open over 50 new stores in its current financial year as part of a £600 million ($793 million) investment, seeking a bigger slice of Britain's grocery market. The group, which in May overtook Morrisons to become Britain's fifth largest grocer, reported a 9.9% increase in 2025/26 operating profit, on turnover up 10.8%, helped by over 40 new stores. item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: British telecom provider BT Group (BT.L) said on Monday it has acquired broadband operator TalkTalk out of administration. BT said it expects an about £400 million ($528.40 million)cash impact from the deal in fiscal 2027, comprising both consideration and other cash impacts. The company expects a regulatory review of the deal to take place over the coming weeks, pending which TalkTalk and BT will operate separately and continue to compete. ($1 = 0.7570 pounds)

item.title: El presidente español hará una declaración ante rumores de elecciones anticipadas
item.description: El presidente del Gobierno de España, Pedro Sánchez, pronunciará una declaración institucional el lunes a las 9:00 hora local (0700 GMT), anunció La Moncloa, ante la expectativa generalizada de que convoque elecciones generales anticipadas.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: El presidente del Gobierno de España, Pedro Sánchez, pronunciará una declaración institucional el lunes a las 9:00 hora local (0700 GMT), anunció La Moncloa, ante la expectativa generalizada de que convoque elecciones generales anticipadas. La posible decisión de adelantar las elecciones, a pesar de que estaban previstas para el año que viene, se produciría después de que el viernes el Congreso de los Diputados rechazara la propuesta del Gobierno para frenar la crisis de la vivienda en el país, en un escenario de protestas masivas. "Es lógico convocar elecciones ahora. No habrá un escenario más favorable. Es arriesgado y podría perder el Gobierno, pero, aun así, no creo que vaya a tener un momento mejor", dijo el analista político Eduardo Bayón. Sin embargo, Sánchez ha insistido en repetidas ocasiones en que las elecciones se celebrarían en 2027 y que él completaría el mandato constitucional de cuatro años. Un portavoz del Gobierno se negó a confirmar de antemano la naturaleza del anuncio.

item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Der französische Technologiekonzern Schneider Electric (SCHN.PA) will das US-Softwareunternehmen PTC (PTC.O) für mehr als 20 Milliarden Euro kaufen. Schneider biete 205 Dollar je PTC-Aktie, was einem Aufschlag zum Schlusskurs von 42,3 Prozent entspreche, teilte der Konzern am Montag mit. Damit werde das in Boston ansässige Unternehmen inklusive Schulden mit 23,7 Milliarden Dollar (rund 21 Milliarden Euro) bewertet. Die Transaktion solle durch eine Kombination aus Eigenkapital und neuen Schulden finanziert und im dritten Quartal 2027 abgeschlossen werden. PTC bietet Softwarelösungen für die Entwicklung, Fertigung und Wartung von Produkten in verschiedenen Branchen an und profitiert ebenfalls von einer wachsenden Nachfrage nach KI-gestützten Werkzeugen. Für Schneider Electric wäre der Zukauf ein weiterer Schritt beim Ausbau des Softwaregeschäfts. Im Juni hatte der Konzern die Übernahme von Cognite Holding vereinbart, einem nicht börsennotierten Anbieter von KI-Software und Industriedaten. Schneider Electric war früher vor allem für Industriekomponenten wie Sicherungen und Schutzschalter bekannt. Inzwischen liefert das Unternehmen die grundlegende Infrastruktur für Rechenzentren, von Kühlanlagen und Serverschränken bis hin zu wichtigen Stromverteilungsanlagen. Die große Nachfrage nach Rechenzentren, insbesondere aus den USA, treibt den Gewinn des Konzerns an und bietet eine wachsende Einnahmequelle. Im Juli hatte Schneider Electric nach Rekordergebnissen im ersten Halbjahr seine Umsatzprognose für das Gesamtjahr angehoben. Dabei setzte das Unternehmen auf eine starke Nachfrage nach seiner Industriesoftware und KI-gestützten Werkzeugen.

item.title: Cost pressures and deadlock force Honda to rework India strategy, sources say
item.description: Honda Motor aims to cut costs by as much as a fifth and halve development times under its new partnership in India with Tata Technologies , according to two people familiar with the matter, as pressure from rivals forces the Japanese automaker to rethink its go-it-alone approach.
item.dc:creator: Aditi Shah, Maki Shiraki
item.content:encoded: Honda Motor (7267.T) aims to cut costs by as much as a fifth and halve development times under its new partnership in India with Tata Technologies (TATE.NS) , according to two people familiar with the matter, as pressure from rivals forces the Japanese automaker to rethink its go-it-alone approach. Reeling from electric vehicle (EV)-related losses that it expects to reach more than $12 billion, Honda is pivoting to gasoline-electric hybrids and slashing expenses. Last month, [USN:L4N44S0E9 TEXT:"Reuters reported"] that it is seeking to cut more than $9 billion in costs over the next four years and has told suppliers to drastically reduce prices. In May, engineering firm Tata Technologies said it was selected to develop vehicles for a Japanese automaker. It declined to name the partner, but the two people and another person familiar with the matter said it was Honda. Under the outsourcing agreement, Tata Technologies will develop cars for the Indian market, while Honda expects to see up to 20% in cost reductions and halve its development times from around five years at present, two people said. Honda decided to bring in Tata Technologies after the automaker's Japanese and Indian managers failed to agree on which suppliers to use for upcoming vehicles in India, two of the people said. All three sources declined to be identified because the information has not been made public. The cost-cutting and development targets in India, as well as the internal deadlock over supplier strategy, are being reported for the first time. In a statement, Honda said it has not been able to offer a sufficient product line-up in India that allows customers "value for money." To that end, it was "redefining" its offerings in India and planned to introduce vehicles that strike a balance between quality and price, it said. It denied there were disagreements between the Japanese and Indian teams over supplier selection. In a separate statement, Honda India said product development involved close collaboration between different teams, adding that it was inaccurate to characterise collaborative discussions as disagreements. Tata Technologies did not respond to a request for comment. STRATEGY DEADLOCK Japanese managers wanted to retain established suppliers to ensure quality and consistency, while Honda's team in India pushed for greater use of local suppliers to lower costs and speed up development in the world's third-largest car market, two of the people said. Reuters could not determine how long the deadlock lasted but the disagreement was enough to delay work on some products, the two people said. The partnership had been under discussion for about two years before being finalised, one of them added. Tata Technologies, which was spun off from Indian automaker Tata Motors (TAMO.NS) , was chosen because of its access to a broad network of local suppliers and because Honda managers believed it could design vehicles in line with consumer tastes and spending preferences, the person said. Honda will oversee the process to ensure quality standards are met and will retain control over areas like technology, connectivity and driver-assistance systems, the person added. FAMOUS INDEPENDENCE Honda has long carried the imprint of its famously independent late founder, Soichiro Honda. It developed two of the world's best-selling cars, the Civic and the Accord, along with the most popular motorcycle of all time, the Super Cub. Like other Japanese automakers, Honda faces the difficult balancing act of defending its legacy business in places like the US while developing new technologies to compete with Chinese firms elsewhere. India, a fast-growing market that remains closed to Chinese EV makers, has become more important. But Honda's market share there has slumped to 1.3% from a peak of 7.3% more than a decade ago. Its portfolio has shrunk to four models and it is losing to affordable, feature-packed rivals like Tata Motors and Mahindra (MAHM.NS) . It also has little to offer in the biggest and fastest-growing SUV segment. "Honda is already late and behind competitors," one of the people said. Honda President Toshihiro Mibe is under pressure to turn around the automaker, which recorded its first-ever annual loss in the last financial year. In May, Mibe said that while India was a "key focus" for Honda, the automaker had not always been successful there. "We need to rebuild the business on an entirely different footing," he said. Previously, Honda adapted for India cars that were originally designed for Japan or other global markets. That resulted in it offering vehicles that were seen as over-engineered and pricey. The first vehicle under development with Tata Technologies is a small SUV that is less than 4 metres (13.1 feet) in length, a segment that accounts for a large portion of India's car market and where Honda has limited presence. It is targeted for launch in 2028, two of the people said. A second, mid-size SUV is expected to follow, with Honda later trying to revive its strength in sedans, one of them added. In its statement, Honda said it planned to launch vehicles in India in the sub-4-metre category and the larger midsize category from 2028 onwards. India is Honda's only major emerging market and it wants to make manufacturing and sourcing there more competitive. If the first product under the deal is successful in terms of quality, sales and profitability, it will open opportunities for Honda to export from India, one of the people said.

item.title: POINT MARCHÉS L'Europe vue dans le désordre, focus sur l'obligataire et l'euro
item.description: Les principales Bourses européennes sont attendues en ordre dispersé lundi à l'ouverture, les investisseurs restant attentifs aux turbulences sur le marché obligataire, particulièrement aiguës en France, tout en surveillant l'euro en difficulté et réajustant leurs prévisions concernant les taux d'intérêt après un rapport sur l'emploi aux États-Unis plus faible que prévu.
item.dc:creator: Diana Mandia
item.content:encoded: Les principales Bourses européennes sont attendues en ordre dispersé lundi à l'ouverture, les investisseurs restant attentifs aux turbulences sur le marché obligataire, particulièrement aiguës en France, tout en surveillant l'euro en difficulté et réajustant leurs prévisions concernant les taux d'intérêt après un rapport sur l'emploi aux États-Unis plus faible que prévu. D'après les premières indications disponibles, le CAC 40 parisien (.FCHI) pourrait perdre 0,11% à l'ouverture. Les contrats à terme signalent une hausse de 0,07% pour le Dax à Francfort (.GDAXI) , de 0,31% pour le FTSE à Londres (.FTSE) et de 0,19% pour le Stoxx 600 (.STOXX) . Les opérateurs reviennent après une semaine marquée par une nouvelle hausse des rendements des obligations souveraines à l'échelle mondiale, alimentée par les craintes inflationnistes liées au Moyen-Orient et les doutes concernant les finances publiques des principales économies mondiales, mais les chiffres de l'emploi aux États-Unis les amènent à revoir, au moins en partie, certaines prévisions. Les données publiées vendredi montrent que la création d'emplois en septembre a été inférieure aux prévisions, tandis que les chiffres de juillet et août ont été révisés à la baisse, ce qui, selon les marchés, réduit à néant la perspective d'une nouvelle hausse des coûts d'emprunt par la Réserve fédérale (Fed) ce mois-ci. "La situation de l'emploi est globalement stable, mais les révisions à la baisse de vendredi indiquent que l'économie américaine a perdu des emplois au cours de deux des neuf mois écoulés depuis le début de l'année, et le risque de nouvelles pertes d'emplois signifie que la Fed ne peut pas relever ses taux de 100 points de base supplémentaires par rapport à leur niveau actuel, ce que la courbe des taux anticipe", déclare Jose Torres, économiste chez Interactive Brokers. Selon l'outil FedWatch de CME, les investisseurs estiment que la probabilité d'une hausse des taux par la Fed ce mois-ci est désormais inférieure à 20%, contre 64% il y a une semaine. Les opérateurs continuent toutefois de miser sur un relèvement en décembre. Les craintes d'inflation ont dominé les marchés ces dernières semaines des deux côtés de l'Atlantique, mettant encore davantage sous pression le marché obligataire et entraînant une forte volatilité des rendements, qui ont atteint des nouveaux sommets aux Etats-Unis et dans la zone euro. En France, où s'ajoute en outre un projet de budget 2027 à l'issue est incertaine, l'écart de rendement entre l'OAT et le Bund allemand à 10 ans évolue autour des 140 points de base (pdb), à un plus haut depuis 2012. La monnaie européenne, déjà affectée par un dollar plus fort dans un contexte de hausse des taux, subit les conséquences de ces incertitudes, alors que les opérateurs évaluent les risques de contagion vers d'autres marchés d'actifs de la zone euro. "Ces inquiétudes concernant les perspectives de l'euro s'ajoutent à celles liées au faible niveau des stocks de gaz en Europe, aux prix déjà élevés de l'énergie, à la concurrence persistante de la Chine, à l'affaiblissement du chancelier allemand et au risque d'attaques hybrides de la part de la Russie" souligne, Jane Foley, analyste chez Rabobank. Les investisseurs attendent par ailleurs les indices PMI définitifs sur l'activité du secteur privé de la zone euro plus tard dans la séance. Outre le suivi constant de l'évolution de la situation au Moyen-Orient, le marché se tourne également vers [USN:L8N45R001 TEXT:"le Brésil,"] où le sénateur de droite Flavio Bolsonaro est arrivé en tête du premier tour de l'élection présidentielle après une campagne marquée par des scandales de corruption, l'inquiétude à propos du coût de la vie et des accusations d'ingérence américaine. LES VALEURS À SUIVRE : [USN:L8N45O1G2] À WALL STREET La Bourse de New York a clôturé vendredi en hausse après l'annonce d'un nombre de créations d'emplois aux Etats-Unis bien moindre que prévu. L'indice Dow Jones (.DJI) a gagné 0,49%, le Standard & Poor's 500 (.SPX) , plus large, a pris 0,73%, et le Nasdaq Composite (.IXIC) a avancé de son côté de 1,19%. EN ASIE L'indice Nikkei (.N225) de la Bourse de Tokyo gagne 2,18%, porté par les valeurs liées à l'intelligence artificielle (IA), dans le sillage de Wall Street vendredi dernier. Le vice-gouverneur de la Banque du Japon (BoJ), Shinichi Uchida, a pour sa part déclaré lundi que l'essor de l'IA avait peut-être assoupli les conditions financières en stimulant la demande et en faisant grimper les cours des actifs, mais il a mis en garde contre le risque d'un recul si les bénéfices attendus ne se concrétisaient pas. Les Bourses de Chine continentale sont fermées jusqu'au 7 octobre à l'occasion des vacances de la Fête nationale. La Bourse de Hong Kong (.HSI) recule de 0,09%. TAUX / CHANGES Le rendement des Treasuries à dix ans recule de 1,3 point de base à 5,2644%, tandis que celui du titre à deux ans perd 2,5 points de base à 4,7996%. Les rendements longs restent toutefois proches de leur plus haut niveau en 24 ans atteint la semaine dernière. Au Japon, le rendement des obligations d'État à 30 ans a atteint un niveau record lundi, dans l'attente de l'allocution de la Première ministre Sanae Takaichi lors de l'ouverture d'une session parlementaire extraordinaire prévue plus tard dans la journée. Sur le marché des changes, le dollar gagne 0,41% face à un panier de devises de référence (.DXY) , malgré la révision à la baisse des paris sur la réunion de la Fed ce mois-ci. L'euro est en difficulté, reculant de 0,59% à 1,1187 dollar , dans un contexte de doutes sur les finances publiques françaises. PÉTROLE Les cours du pétrole reculent légèrement, l'augmentation des exportations en provenance du Moyen-Orient et la mise sur le marché de stocks par les pays du G7 ayant accru l'offre. Le Brent recule de 0,54% à 101,70 dollars le baril et le brut léger américain (West Texas Intermediate, WTI) perd 1,15% à 90,06 dollars. L'impasse persiste toutefois au Moyen-Orient. Le détroit d'Ormuz ne sera pas rouvert tant que les sept conditions iraniennes énoncées dans l'accord provisoire conclu en juin avec les Etats-Unis n'auront pas été remplies, [USN:L8N45Q03U TEXT:"a déclaré"] dimanche le président du Parlement iranien, Mohammad Baqer Qalibaf, cité par le média iranien Nournews. L'Opep+ a par ailleurs [USN:L8N45Q03Z TEXT:"décidé"] de maintenir ses objectifs de production de pétrole pour novembre, a déclaré l'organisation dans un communiqué publié à l'issue de sa réunion de ce dimanche. item.title: Deutsche Telekom sees €2.5 billion in savings from AI, automation by 2030
item.description: Deutsche Telekom said on Monday it expected to save around €2.5 billion ($2.8 billion) in indirect costs by 2030 compared to 2023, as the German telecommunications group expands its use of AI and automation.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Deutsche Telekom (DTEGn.DE) said on Monday it expected to save around [USN:FWN45R02Y TEXT:"€2.5 billion"] ($2.8 billion) in indirect costs by 2030 compared to 2023, as the German telecommunications group expands its use of AI and automation. "AI detects peak traffic on the cellular network earlier, supports customer service representatives, and thus helps resolve issues immediately," Deutsche Telekom said in a statement. In 2027, AI and automation are estimated to generate gross savings of around €1.1 billion outside the US compared to 2023 The company intends to partly invest additional 2027 savings in Germany's digital infrastructure and fibre-optic network It sees a "major business opportunity" in Europe's goal to develop sovereign AI It also aims to increase AI-related revenue from business with companies outside the US to around €800 million by 2030 Deutsche Telekom confirmed its 2026 outlook and medium-term targets ($1 = €0.8941)

item.title: Deutsche Telekom erhofft sich Milliarden-Einsparungen durch KI
item.description: Die Deutsche Telekom will durch den verstärkten Einsatz Künstlicher Intelligenz (KI) kräftig sparen. Im kommenden Jahr würden die Kosten im Vergleich zu 2023 voraussichtlich um 1,1 Milliarden Euro sinken, teilte der Bonner Konzern am Montag mit. Bis 2030 werde die Ersparnis auf 2,5 Milliarden Euro steigen. Die Ausgaben für die Nutzung dieser Technologie seien bei dieser Berechnung allerdings nicht berücksichtigt. Gleichzeitig prognostizierte die Telekom ein kräftiges Wachstum ihres KI-Geschäfts. Die entsprechenden Umsätze außerhalb der USA würden bis 2030 auf rund 800 Millionen von derzeit etwa 250 Millionen Euro anwachsen.

item.content:encoded: Die Deutsche Telekom (DTEGn.DE) will durch den verstärkten Einsatz Künstlicher Intelligenz (KI) kräftig sparen. Im kommenden Jahr würden die Kosten im Vergleich zu 2023 voraussichtlich um 1,1 Milliarden Euro sinken, teilte der Bonner Konzern am Montag mit. Bis 2030 werde die Ersparnis auf 2,5 Milliarden Euro steigen. Die Ausgaben für die Nutzung dieser Technologie seien bei dieser Berechnung allerdings nicht berücksichtigt. Gleichzeitig prognostizierte die Telekom ein kräftiges Wachstum ihres KI-Geschäfts. Die entsprechenden Umsätze außerhalb der USA würden bis 2030 auf rund 800 Millionen von derzeit etwa 250 Millionen Euro anwachsen. "KI verändert die Telekom von Grund auf", sagte Konzernchef Tim Höttges. "Sie macht unsere Netze besser und eröffnet neue Geschäftsmodelle, vom KI-Assistenten im Telefonat bis zur souveränen Infrastruktur für Europas Industrie." Die Deutsche Telekom betreibt unter anderem ein [USN:L8N3Z01MT TEXT:"KI-Rechenzentrum"] in München. Sie entwickelt darüber hinaus eigenen Angaben zufolge eine Plattform für den Mittelstand, um wiederkehrende Aufgaben zu automatisieren. Ein digitaler Assistent soll künftig Gespräche in Echtzeit übersetzen, ihre Inhalte zusammenfassen oder Fragen dazu beantworten können. Intern helfe die KI, drohende Belastungsspitzen oder Störungen im Netz frühzeitig zu erkennen, hieß es weiter. Sie unterstütze zudem die Software-Entwicklung und entlaste den Kundendienst. Die Telekom will einen Teil der Einsparungen in den Ausbau ihres Glasfasernetzes stecken. Das Unternehmen gab die KI-Strategie anlässlich seines ersten, dieser Technologie gewidmeten Investorentags bekannt. Auf der Veranstaltung sollen unter anderem praktische Anwendungsbeispiele präsentiert werden.

item.title: As Iran war smolders, shunned Eritrea looks to come in from the cold
item.description: When Halima Mohammed was six, her parents dropped her off in the desert at Revolution School, where the children of Eritrean guerrilla fighters were raised while their parents fought for independence.
item.dc:creator: Giulia Paravicini
item.content:encoded: When Halima Mohammed was six, her parents dropped her off in the desert at Revolution School, where the children of Eritrean guerrilla fighters were raised while their parents fought for independence. Wounded fighters taught grammar when they weren't carrying rifles. Mothers and fathers appeared only rarely before melting back into the mountains and deserts of a war that would rage for three decades before Eritrea seceded from Ethiopia in 1993. Halima, 56, is now education minister of Eritrea, where that revolutionary struggle still hangs heavily over one of the most secluded and regimented societies on Earth. She presides over a schooling system that binds the future of the country's children into the service of the state. All teenagers must undergo army training towards the end of high school before being assigned mandatory and often indefinitely long roles in the military or in national service, mainly low-paid civilian jobs like teaching and policing. "All school graduates are getting at least a job to work, and they are getting their salary. And at the same time, they are serving the country," Halima told Reuters, which was granted rare access to the nation. "If you are going to have more freedom, first you have to have a country, you have to have national security, because we paid a lot for Eritrea." Eritrea has long been isolated by the West, which views the East African country as among the most repressive in the world, while the government in Asmara has itself pursued a policy of political and economic seclusion. No elections have been held since the nation became a sovereign state in the 1990s. Independent media outlets were shut down in 2001. Hundreds of thousands of Eritreans have defied strict travel restrictions, which bar most working-age citizens from leaving the country, to abscond overseas. This small country of fewer than 4 million people has nonetheless acquired new geopolitical significance this year, during the Iran war, owing to its 1,000 km coastline along the Red Sea shipping route between the Mediterranean and Asia. The route has proved a [USN:L8N4081EB TEXT:"critical alternative"] to the Strait of Hormuz, which was the primary export route for Gulf energy shipments before it was effectively closed by the conflict. Attacks on Red Sea trading vessels by Iran-backed Houthi militants in Yemen, which faces Eritrea across the route's southern chokepoint, have made Eritrean waters potentially the most secure transit corridor. "Eritrea sits astride some of the world's hottest geographical real estate," said Murithi Mutiga, Africa program director at the International Crisis Group, a Brussels-based think-tank. "The war in the Gulf has highlighted the importance of the Red Sea as an alternative outlet for that region. It's no wonder outside powers are courting Asmara." There have been signs of warming ties with the world: Last week, Washington removed its sanctions on Eritrea, which were imposed over the role of the country's military in the Tigray conflict in Ethiopia in 2020-22. The State Department said the Trump administration made the decision "to advance US regional interests." Reuters interviewed several senior government figures during a recent trip to Eritrea, as well as dozens of Eritreans at home and abroad, to piece together a picture of a society largely walled off from the modern world. The officials pressed a consistent message: Eritrea is ready to engage and trade, they said. It is prepared to open up to investors keen to tap its gold, copper and potash. It is looking at reforming its school system to give young people more say over their destiny. Yet beneath these aspirations lies a state shaped by its leaders' iron conviction that national survival depends on stringent internal security and military vigilance against Ethiopia, its larger neighbor. In recent years, the countries have been at loggerheads over landlocked Ethiopia's demands that Eritrea grant it commercial and naval access to the Red Sea, particularly the port of Assab near their border. Ethiopia, which had access to the coastline for decades before Eritrea broke away, has cast maritime access as a matter of urgent national security. Meanwhile, Asmara has said it fears Addis Ababa will try to take Assab by force. Getachew Reda, the Ethiopian premier's adviser on regional affairs, said Addis Ababa has never threatened to use force or violate Eritrea's sovereignty. He said that Eritrea poses a security threat because of its readiness to fund insurgencies within Ethiopia, an allegation denied by Asmara. Getachew said access to the Red Sea is a matter of economic necessity for Ethiopia, a country of 130 million people, and that his government is willing to come to a peaceful arrangement with Eritrea such as a long-term lease deal on the use of ports. Last week, the countries [USN:L6N45N0FE TEXT:"cut diplomatic ties"], with Ethiopia expelling Eritrean diplomats and Asmara retaliating. Eritrea has not always been isolated from the West; it enjoyed friendly relations with the US and several European nations in the years following its independence before diplomatic ties collapsed in 2001 when Asmara cracked down on political opponents and journalists. THE CAPITAL ABOVE THE CLOUDS Asmara, Eritrea's highland capital, seems a city suspended in time. Elderly men, many of them veterans with wheelchairs or crutches, linger over macchiatos at dusk beneath fading Italian signs at Bar Vittoria and Bar America, legacies of the Italian colonial rule that preceded Ethiopian control. Tightly controlled internet access is sparse and slow. Few people bother staring at phones. Young people drink unlabeled bottles of beer from the state-owned factory. Almost no cars can be seen on the streets amid severe government fuel rationing, save a few battered taxis that have survived in an economy ground down by decades of Western sanctions. Even as ministers spoke of reform and engagement, many ordinary Eritreans remained reluctant to discuss politics. Conversations often end the same way. A glance over the shoulder. A lowered voice. A polite smile. "It's better not to," several people said when questions turned to national service or political freedoms. Others only agreed to speak if they weren't identified. Walking through a residential district of Asmara, the sound of applause drifted out from an old cinema. An information session for Sawa was underway. Little epitomizes the tensions tearing at the fabric of the nation more than Sawa, a remote military camp in the desert near the border with Sudan. This is where teenagers must go to complete their final year of secondary school and undergo military training. In the cinema, rows of teenagers due to leave home for Sawa faced a stage where a young woman clicked through a PowerPoint presentation filled with photos of students in camouflage uniforms, marching in formation and studying in classrooms. The presenter, 24-year-old Luna Ermias, wore jeans, sunglasses pushed onto her head and braces that flashed when she smiled. She spoke passionately. "I was there in 2019," she told Reuters afterwards. "It teaches you to rely on yourself. You manage your money, your time. You meet people from every part of Eritrea." ESCAPING ACROSS A BURNING DESERT Many don't share her enthusiasm. Muse said he was 17 when he decided he would rather run than report to Sawa. He felt sure if he stayed, his life would never be his own. He packed almost nothing. He slipped away from home under the cover of darkness, hoping to cross the border with Ethiopia before the authorities caught him. He didn't make it. Muse said he spent the next six months in prison. When he was released, he added, he wasn't sent home. He was instead deployed in the military to Assab, the Red Sea port. He escaped again. This time he succeeded. He crossed the blistering Danakil desert into Ethiopia before reaching another East African country, where Reuters interviewed him. The journey cost him thousands of dollars paid to smugglers, money borrowed from relatives already living abroad. Reuters reviewed Muse's asylum documents and spoke to three family members who corroborated his story. The news agency couldn't independently verify all elements of the account given by the teenager, who asked for his full name and location to be withheld. His story isn't unique. According to the United Nations, more than 679,000 Eritreans are living as refugees or asylum seekers abroad, a significant chunk of the nation's small population. Human Rights Watch and many other rights groups say the prospect of prolonged compulsory service has driven generations of young people to flee, often risking perilous journeys across the Sahara and Mediterranean. The Eritrean government did not comment on the details of Muse's account, though said asylum seekers normally fabricate claims to be granted asylum. The government disputed the UN figures, saying a significant portion of those classed as refugees are actually from neighboring countries who posed as Eritreans to secure fast-tracked asylum and social benefits. It said Eritrean youths were not primarily driven away by national service but rather drawn abroad by external factors including economic incentives, family reunifications and generous asylum policies in the West. Germany, Switzerland, Sweden, Britain and the US are among the most popular Western destinations for Eritrean refugees and asylum seekers, according to the UN. DREAMING OF MERCEDES-BENZ Not everyone who wants to leave manages to do so. In Asmara, Reuters met a mechanical engineer who was among Sawa students to achieve top grades and was therefore allowed to attend university. He spoke avidly about German engineering. He'd dreamed of working for Mercedes-Benz one day. Instead, he was assigned to a government job as an auto mechanic. "You don't study what you want," he said. "Even if you finish university, you often don't work in your field." At around 2,300 Nakfa ($153) a month, he said, his salary barely covers basic necessities. Saving enough to pay smugglers or finance a life abroad felt impossible. Officials in Asmara maintained that Western governments and rights groups have long misrepresented Eritrea's national service program by overlooking the security pressures the country faces from Ethiopia, with which it shares one of Africa's most turbulent relationships. Eritrea emerged from the 30-year independence war, which killed tens of thousands on both sides, only to fight another devastating border conflict with its neighbor seven years later. Persistent regional violence has further cemented a sense of permanent mobilization inside the young state. Halima, the girl left in the desert a lifetime ago, now sits behind a polished wooden desk in the Ministry of Education in Asmara, housed in the striking red Casa del Fascio, built during colonial rule as the Eritrean headquarters of Italy's National Fascist Party. With four children of her own, she doesn't dismiss the frustrations of young Eritreans. Her ultimate goal, she says, is to replace compulsory national service with vocational colleges and technical schools. But all plans are subordinate to national security. "First we have to think about Eritrea. We have to protect it," she said. "As a mother, first I have to think about Eritrea."

item.title: For freed Israeli hostages, every moment is now precious
item.description: Taken with their children or alone. Held for weeks, months or years. Confined in captors' homes or Hamas tunnels as war raged above them. Israeli former hostages seized on October 7 say they now cherish even the smallest moments of freedom.
item.dc:creator: Shir Torem, Hannah Confino
item.content:encoded: Taken with their children or alone. Held for weeks, months or years. Confined in captors' homes or Hamas tunnels as war raged above them. Israeli former hostages seized on October 7 say they now cherish even the smallest moments of freedom. Hamas' October 7, 2023, attack was Israel's single deadliest day. The militants rampaged through villages, a music festival and army bases, killing 1,200 people and dragging 251 hostages back to Gaza. They included civilians, soldiers, men, women, children and elderly people, Israelis and foreign nationals. Most were freed in return for Palestinian prisoners during ceasefires between Israel and Hamas, but dozens did not survive. "Freedom has completely changed the way I see life," said Emily Damari, 30, who was abducted wounded from her home in Kibbutz Kfar Aza and released in January 2025. Her ordeal taught her not to take anything for granted, she said. "One day in captivity feels like one week. You want to give up at every moment, but I did not," said Damari, who has recently married and launched a clothing line in Israel. "Today, I open the fridge and I say thank you. I drink cold water and I say thank you. I am thankful for everything, big things and little things. Gratitude has become central to who I am," said Damari. "Being free, at home, surrounded by my family and my people is something I will never take for granted again." "I CHOOSE LIFE" Eli Sharabi, 54, was seized from nearby Kibbutz Be'eri. His British-born wife Lianne and their two daughters Noiya, 16, and Yahel, 13, were slain by the attackers. His brother Yossi was taken hostage and killed in Gaza. In February 2025, Sharabi was released, appearing emaciated and skeletally thin, from 491 days of captivity which he says included being held in a tunnel, hungry, shackled and beaten. "I learned in captivity how precious every moment and every choice can be, and I carry that understanding with me now. I choose to look ahead, to keep going and to use the life I have in a meaningful way," said Sharabi. Since his release he has helped establish the Shalva Sharabi Family Centre in the southern city of Ashkelon with the disability charity Shalva, to treat families coping with trauma and disabilities, in commemoration of his own family lost. "I choose life. I choose to keep living fully, while carrying Lianne, Noiya, Yahel and Yossi with me in everything I do." His wife and daughters believed deeply in caring for others, he said. "Their kindness and care for others will continue. Families will walk through these doors and receive help, care and hope in a place that carries their name. That gives me strength and makes me very proud," said Sharabi. SLOWLY BUILDING A FUTURE Hagar Brodutch was seized from Kfar Aza with her three children and her neighbours' daughter who fled to their house after her parents were killed. They were freed in a brief truce in November 2023. Life after captivity, she said, can be far more complicated than sometimes portrayed. "The daily struggle is immense, especially for children. I believe it will take many more years before captivity becomes just a shadow that walks alongside us, rather than something that defines who we are," said Brodutch. Recently, Brodutch, 43, has begun taking classes in pastry baking, for which she has long had a passion. "This is about much more than learning how to bake. It is about finding a new path, creating something with my own hands, and slowly building a future," she said. "During my time in Hamas captivity, I began to understand that if I were released, returning to my previous life and working in management might no longer be possible," said Brodutch. "I chose pastry as a form of therapy, but also as a way to create something new for myself, with the hope that one day it could become my profession," she said. Kfar Aza was one of the hardest-hit communities in Hamas' attack. Aviva Siegel, 65, was kidnapped with her husband Keith. She was released in November 2023, but Keith was held until February 2025. Aviva joined the hostage release campaign movement in Israel while her husband was still being held. Their reunion and her children and grandchildren, and even strangers she meets, give her strength every day, she says. "I feel that I’m not alone and that there's so much love in this world and we need to keep it with both our hands," she said. "I feel very, very lucky to be alive."

item.title: Hong Kong’s New World backstop looks shrewd
item.description: The government could own a 30% stake in the city's most indebted developer as part of a project termination deal. It could help reassure creditors ahead of New World's imminent $8 bln debt restructuring and bolster its finances to invest in Hong Kong's Northern Metropolis plan.
item.dc:creator: Ka Sing Chan
item.content:encoded: For the first time ever, the Hong Kong government could become a major shareholder in one of the city's major property developers. The Airport Authority has an option to buy a near-30% stake in the Cheng family's $2 billion New World Development (0017.HK) , as part of an early termination agreement over a mega entertainment, retail and commercial project. That prospect could reassure creditors including HSBC (HSBA.L) ahead of the developer's looming debt restructuring. But the government is stepping into uncharted territory. The deal , unveiled on Wednesday along with annual results, gives the embattled New World a huge helping hand. The company will pay HK$2.3 billion, roughly $300 million, in cash to the Airport Authority so that the developer can walk away from a 50-year agreement to build and operate 11 SKIES, an ambitious complex next to the city's airport. That, along with impairment losses and other provisions, pushed New World's bottom line HK$28.1 billion into the red for the year to the end of June. The upside is that the company, which owns the luxury Rosewood hotel and a raft of malls and office buildings in Hong Kong, is now freed from paying out yearly lease obligations of HK$1.8 billion - up to 30% of its estimated annual revenue, per analysts at Citi - for the next four decades. The more consequential part of the agreement, arguably, is the Airport Authority's three-year call option to acquire 750 million New World shares for HK$2.3 billion - essentially refunding the termination fee for a 30% stake. The government-owned commercial entity is getting an implied 50% discount to the stock's undisturbed price; the Cheng family, meanwhile, has already stated it will remain New World's single largest and controlling shareholder. Having the government appear to be a backstop may help accelerate the real-estate giant's debt cleanup. The company has some $8.2 billion in loans and bonds coming due over the next two years that are all but certain to require restructuring with creditors, on top of last year's $11 billion refinancing with banks including HSBC and Bank of China (601988.SS) . Notably, on the same day as the 11 SKIES deal was announced, New World also said that its loan facility with Deutsche Bank (DBKGn.DE) increased to HK$4.9 billion, from the HK$3.95 billion committed in June. Even so, the Airport Authority's option leaves a lot of uncertainty. Government support is at best implicit and it's not clear under what conditions officials will choose to take a stake and what role they will play in New World. Strategically, the developer is investing in the Northern Metropolis, a flagship project in Hong Kong's Five-Year Plan meant to expand housing supply and create a new economic engine along the Shenzhen border. The government has opted to be a stakeholder in New World's revival rather than squeezing it for maximum compensation. Whether that proves a bargain depends on its coming debt overhaul. New World Development said on September 30 it will terminate its contractual agreements for 11 SKIES, a mega airport mall, with Hong Kong's Airport Authority by paying an early termination fee of HK$2.3 billion ($295 million), and provide works and services worth up to HK$1.1 billion for free. As part of the deal, the Airport Authority also has an option to acquire 750 million shares in New World, representing roughly 30% of the total, for HK$2.3 billion, within three years. As a result of this agreement, New World recorded a net loss of HK$18.3 billion related to the 11 SKIES project in the year ending June, which included HK$14.7 billion in impairment losses as well as the early termination costs and provisions. item.title: October 7 families join election race with hope of healing Israel
item.description: One was inspired by her son's last stand trying to fight off attackers rampaging through a kibbutz. Another by her son's final words as militants tossed grenades into a bomb shelter packed with fleeing revellers from a music festival. A third by the brothers he campaigned to bring home from captivity in Gaza.
item.dc:creator: Maayan Lubell, Emily Rose
item.content:encoded: One was inspired by her son's last stand trying to fight off attackers rampaging through a kibbutz. Another by her son's final words as militants tossed grenades into a bomb shelter packed with fleeing revellers from a music festival. A third by the brothers he campaigned to bring home from captivity in Gaza. Three years since Hamas' October 7 attack, at least nine Israelis from families directly caught up in the deadliest day in the country's history are running for parliament in an election this month. They represent parties running the gamut of political views, but all say they aim to heal Israel's wounds. The militants who burst into southern Israel in 2023 killed 1,200 people and took 251 hostages to Gaza. Michal Hirsch Negri's son, Roee, died fighting Hamas attackers in Kibbutz Be'eri, where 1 in 10 residents were killed. Soon after the surprise attack began, Roee, newly married and on a career path in high-tech, scrambled comrades in his reserve counter-terrorism military unit, who later recounted their last moments with him. "He told them: 'We are not looking at the bodies. We are here to save people. We are here to save our country.' And this is a sentence that is engraved in my heart," said his mother. Hirsch Negri, 60, is running in Together, led by former Prime Minister Naftali Bennett and part of an alliance of left, right and centre parties aiming to oust Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's nationalist-religious coalition. "Everyone knows what's bad. Everyone knows what is broken. Talking about how bad it is or how bad the government is won't get us anywhere. My Roee, he always looked at the situation, analysed it and said, okay, now what can we do to fix it?" 'ON A MISSION' One of her running mates is Noam Tibon, 64, a former general whose son was trapped with his young family in their home on Nahal Oz, another kibbutz attacked by Hamas. Tibon and his wife set out from Tel Aviv to rescue their son, battling en route with Hamas militants and evacuating wounded to hospital. "October 7 was the biggest failure in our history and I saw it with my own eyes," he said. Netanyahu has rejected blame for the security breach and resisted [USN:L8N3XU0CX TEXT:"calls for an independent investigation"]. Sharon Sharabi, 51, running in the right-wing Israel Our Home party, says he witnessed Israel's leadership failings when he [USN:L8N3EM7UO TEXT:"campaigned for a deal to free Gaza hostages"], including his brothers Yossi and Eli, both seized by Hamas from Be'eri. Yossi [USN:L1N3E508T TEXT:"did not survive captivity"]. Eli, whose wife and two teenage daughters were slain in the kibbutz, was [USN:L1N3OY15C TEXT:"released in early 2025"] after [USN:L5N3P80TO TEXT:"almost 500 days"]. "I understood that even after the hostages come back, that I can't stand aside and let mediocre people keep running the country," Sharabi said. "I understood that I have to leave my life behind, to go on a mission to remedy, to return the state of Israel to its true values." Not all see removing the coalition as the path forward. Talik Gvili, whose police officer son Ran was [USN:L8N3XD08D TEXT:"the last Israeli hostage whose remains were recovered from Gaza"], was personally chosen by Netanyahu as a candidate on his party's slate. "I am continuing the mission Rani was on. He went to defend Israel," she said in a party campaign video. "I want a strong leader, someone I can count on," she said of Netanyahu. "He promised to bring Rani home and he did. He promised to make a change in the Middle East and he did." 'CONTINUE AFTER ME' But most of the candidates from October 7 families support parties aligned against Netanyahu, driven by what they see as failings on that day and since. Shira Shapiro, 51, is running as a candidate for Yashar, a new opposition centrist party led by former military chief Gadi Eisenkot whose own soldier son was killed in Gaza. Shapiro said she and other parents of October 7 victims "are trying to take this pain and give it meaning, to grow from it. This is also what we need to do on a national level." Her eldest son Aner, a 22-year-old off-duty soldier and musician, had attended the Nova music festival attacked on October 7 and took cover with 26 others in [USN:L8N3DY1WS TEXT:"a roadside bomb shelter"]. As the Hamas men lobbed grenades into the packed shelter, Aner tossed them out. His last moments were caught in dashcam footage, an audio recording made by one of the victims before she was killed and a photo taken by a survivor. Aner told the others that if he is hurt, they must continue. "I hear his voice say 'continue after me', he meant continue throwing the grenades but I hear his voice saying 'continue after me'," said Shapiro. "And I have to continue after him. And that's why I'm here."

item.title: Ukraine scrambles for money to fight war as Russian strikes batter economy
item.description: Kryvyi Rih, the hometown of Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy, is struggling to survive. Russian airstrikes have brought the city's huge steel plant and mines to a standstill, dragging the local economy to its knees.
item.dc:creator: Olena Harmash
item.content:encoded: Kryvyi Rih, the hometown of Ukrainian President [USN:L8N45P03V TEXT:"Volodymyr Zelenskiy"], is struggling to survive. Russian airstrikes have brought the city's huge steel plant and mines to a standstill, dragging the local economy to its knees. Mayor Oleksandr Vilkul said the sprawling industrial city — which stretches along the banks of the Inhulets River — was doing everything possible to ensure its hospitals remain open, the lights remain on in kindergartens and schools, and buses keep running. "In Kryvyi Rih, the situation is actually worse than anywhere else, apart from the front line itself," Vilkul, 52, a former mining executive, said in a video address. The financial squeeze on the city of about 600,000 people underlines the challenges facing Ukraine as the government navigates its biggest budget crisis since Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022. Last month, the city's largest employer — ArcelorMittal's hulking mining and steelmaking complex — [USN:L1N45H03O TEXT:"suspended its operations"] following a series of Russian ballistic missile strikes that darkened its furnaces. The prospects for next year, Vilkul said, are bleak. "It's about survival. Right now, we need to survive," he said. It's a scene played out across Ukraine's once-mighty steel industry, which accounted for a tenth of economic output before the war. Giant mills in Zaporizhzhia in the southeast and other industrial cities stand silent and exports have stopped. An escalation in [USN:L1N45O02H TEXT:"Russia's drone and missile strikes"] this summer destroyed factories and warehouses across Ukraine, damaged ports and railways, and forced shops and businesses to close, slowing the growth of the economy and tax revenue. Meanwhile, the [USN:L1N42K0E6 TEXT:"technology-driven war"] is becoming ever more expensive for Ukraine to fight. Billions of euros in foreign loans have been delayed by failure to pass bills including unpopular tax reforms and anti-corruption legislation demanded by Ukraine's Western allies, leaving a gaping hole in state coffers. Ukraine needs $56 billion to fund that gap this year —equivalent to about a quarter of its economic output. Of that, $27 billion is military spending. To bridge the shortfall, Ukrainian officials met European partners in Brussels last week to discuss bringing forward disbursements due next year under a €90-billion ($101-billion) EU loan. The [USN:L1N45N0W8 TEXT:"European Commission and Ukraine"] said they had identified funds to close the gap this year. But three sources familiar with the talks said accelerating these payments risked increasing budget pressure next year - at a time when looming election campaigns in European allies including France and Poland could erode support for Kyiv. Prime Minister Sergii Koretskyi acknowledges the situation is "challenging". The government has been forced to freeze non-essential spending — including reconstruction of damaged buildings and infrastructure — to prioritise military spending, public sector wages and pensions. "All resources should be channelled into critically important areas," Koretskyi told reporters. WAR COSTS SOAR, DOMESTIC REVENUES FALL Two years ago, a single day of fighting cost Ukraine $140 million, but that figure has jumped to $190 million, according to Roksolana Pidlasa, the head of parliament's budget committee. And that does not include direct military support to Kyiv from its Western allies. Rising costs are driven partly by the need for expensive medium- and long-range weapons capable of striking [USN:L1N45C00L TEXT:"Russia's oil refineries"] and military factories to reduce Moscow's ability to continue its war. Plus, the wage bill for an expanded army is higher than ever before, and the state must support a growing number of military families of disabled or deceased soldiers. "Expenditure will continue to rise," Pidlasa told a conference in Kyiv. "This is one more pragmatic reason why the US and Europe need to act faster to force (Russia) to end this war." In the first nine months of this year, Ukraine spent more than $44 billion on defence alone, data showed. That does not include in-kind military support from allies. In the same period, the government was able to raise only about $42 billion in tax revenue as the economy slowed. Pidlasa said that in the first nine months of this year Ukraine's budget lost over 49.5 billion hryvnias ($1.1 billion) in tax revenue because of Russian attacks that not only damaged property and goods, but disrupted logistics and shut shops and businesses for hours at a time. By the end of the year, the cumulative losses could rise to 70 billion hryvnias, the government estimates. "We have not a temporary but a structural problem with the revenues at the very time when spending really requires resources," said Oleksandra Myronenko, an economist at the Centre for Economic Strategies, a Kyiv-based think tank. Some Ukrainian businesses have started to scale back operations. Others have put capital expenditure on hold as the country braces for a difficult winter. Business sentiment and economic expectations are darkening. Vasyl Khmelnytskyi, founder of an industrial park in the city of Bila Tserkva near Kyiv, said he had scrapped plans to build three new factories. "The risks are simply too great right now — both for the business and for the people," he said in a Facebook post. [USN:L8N44605L TEXT:"Ukraine's agricultural sector"] — its largest source of export revenues — has been particularly hard hit. Russian attacks on Ukraine's Black Sea ports led to a 36.6% fall in grain exports year-on-year in September. About $40 billion in export revenue is at risk this year as a result of the blockade, Economy Minister Oleksandr Kravchenko said. Even with tens of billions of euros in foreign support, Ukraine's economy is expected to grow only between 0.5% and 1.5% this year, economists say — down from 1.8% in 2025. FOREIGN AID IS DELAYED During more than four years of intense fighting, Ukraine has been able to maintain macroeconomic and financial stability thanks to fiscal support from its Western partners, receiving nearly $200 billion since Russia's invasion. But $29.5 billion in foreign aid is now at risk this year because of delays in passing reforms, Koretskyi said. The government has postponed about $900 million of capital spending until December, in the hope the legislation will be passed. The aim is to pass all the required legislation in parliament by October 15, Koretskyi said. "Only then we will get all the money," Koretskyi said. "This is absolutely vital. It needs to be done as soon as possible." Legislators are now discussing the budget for next year. The government has proposed record defence budget spending of $110 billion. This figure does not include direct military aid. Finance Minister Sergii Marchenko has estimated that the unfunded budget gap for the next year is already more than $32 billion. Part of the solution, Marchenko said, is to use frozen Russian assets in Europe to fund Ukraine's budget. EU countries immobilised some €210 billion of Russian central bank assets after Moscow invaded Ukraine. "Ukraine continues to mobilise domestic resources, but the scale of Russia's war puts clear limits on our capacity," Marchenko said on X. ($1 = 0.8906 euros)

item.title: Huawei agrees to a multi-year patent licensing deal with Qualcomm
item.description: China's Huawei Technologies (HWT.UL) said on Monday it had agreed a broad multi-year patent licence deal with Qualcomm covering artificial intelligence, 5G, computing and networking technologies.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: China's Huawei Technologies (HWT.UL) said on Monday it had agreed a broad multi-year patent licence deal with Qualcomm (QCOM.O) covering artificial intelligence, 5G, computing and networking technologies. Here are some details: The agreement includes Qualcomm's purchase of certain Huawei US patents related to computing, AI and networking, Huawei said in a statement. It is Huawei's first patent licensing deal with Qualcomm that covers 5G technologies. Huawei said the deal is expected to push the total value of its patent licensing agreements to more than $6.9 billion once completed. The company said its intellectual property licensing business has generated positive revenue since 2021, reflecting years of heavy investment in research and development. Huawei ramped up R&D spending in recent years, as US trade restrictions since 2019 have limited its ability to buy advanced chips and crucial software. Huawei made its first licensing payment to Qualcomm in 2001, while it received its first licensing income in 2011 from Motorola. The Qualcomm agreement follows a licensing [USN:L6N44M0N7 TEXT:"deal"] with HP Inc (HPQ.N) announced by Huawei in August.

item.title: Oil's new problem isn't supply. It's logistics
item.description: Middle East crude exports recently climbed to their highest levels since the start of the Iran war as more Gulf producers resume transit through the Strait of Hormuz – despite the continued threat of Iranian attacks. Yet oil prices remain stubbornly elevated, suggesting logistical problems are proving as disruptive as outright supply losses.
item.dc:creator: Ron Bousso
item.content:encoded: Middle East crude exports recently climbed to their highest levels since the start of the Iran war as more Gulf producers resume transit through the [USN:S8N43Z003 TEXT:"Strait of Hormuz"] – despite the continued threat of Iranian attacks. Yet oil prices remain stubbornly elevated, suggesting logistical problems are proving as disruptive as outright supply losses. Crude flows through the embattled waterway reached 14.2 million barrels per day on a seven-day average on Sept. 26, nearly 80% of pre-war levels, according to analytics firm Kpler. While volumes have declined since, they will likely be revised higher because ships often disable satellite tracking systems while traversing the strait and for several days thereafter. Either way, the trend is clear: a lot more crude is getting through the strait. So why is Brent still trading above $100 per barrel? In a word, logistics. For decades, the global oil industry functioned as a finely tuned system designed to move enormous volumes of crude and fuels over long distances at the lowest possible cost. The conflicts in the Middle East and Eastern Europe have fractured that model, as a combination of record-high tanker rates, soaring insurance costs and a severe shortage of refining capacity has created bottlenecks across the energy supply chain. Those problems may take months, if not years, to unwind, leaving consumers facing persistently high energy bills – even if the crude supply squeeze continues to ease. BREAKING THE BLOCKADE Iran's blockade of the Strait of Hormuz following the onset of the war with the US and Israel on February 28 rapidly reshaped global oil flows. Gulf producers diverted supplies through alternative routes, buyers sought barrels from more distant regions and governments released unprecedented volumes of oil from strategic reserves. One of the biggest changes was that Saudi Arabia – previously the world’s largest oil exporter – diverted its exports through its [USN:L4N45E0KG TEXT:"East-West pipeline"], which delivers crude to the Red Sea port of Yanbu. At one point this year, 4% of global oil supplies were via this route. However, after the pipeline came under attack by Iranian-backed Iraqi militias [USN:L6N4590XN TEXT:"in early September"], Saudi Arabia was forced to redirect exports back to the Gulf via Hormuz, which it discovered, could be more easily transited than previously thought. Saudi exports through Hormuz averaged 3 million bpd in September, the highest level during the conflict, according to Kpler. While Saudi Arabia’s crude exports through Hormuz in September were still only around half of pre-war volumes, the Kingdom’s exports could quickly near pre-war levels as the East-West pipeline [USN:L4N45E0KG TEXT:"gradually returns"] to normal operations. Ironically, then, the attack on the East-West pipeline, which was intended to cripple Riyadh, may have instead weakened Tehran's most powerful leverage – its purported control of the Strait – by demonstrating that large volumes can still transit Hormuz and other major export hubs despite continued attacks. GREAT FREIGHT Yet the recovery remains fragile. On the one hand, the increase in Gulf exports has helped reduce the global oil deficit. Energy Aspects estimates the market now faces a shortfall of around 1.6 million bpd, down from roughly 4 million bpd during the peak disruption in May. Under normal circumstances, such an improvement in supply would exert significant downward pressure on prices. Instead, Brent remains above $100 a barrel, more than 40% above pre-war levels. Prices certainly reflect a substantial risk premium linked to the possibility of renewed escalation, as Washington and Tehran have still failed to reach any form of understanding over the future of Hormuz. But geopolitics is only part of the story. Freight and insurance costs, once a relatively minor component of the delivered price of oil, have become major price drivers. This is partly due to the current [USN:L6N45A0SP TEXT:"shuttle system"] operating around the Gulf. Multiple tankers are frequently required to transport crude though Hormuz to the Gulf of Oman, where cargoes are transferred to smaller vessels before heading to buyers in Asia. This ties up significant numbers of very large crude carriers (VLCCs), reducing vessel availability elsewhere. At the same time, buyers are increasingly sourcing crude from the Atlantic Basin and shipping it to Asia over longer routes, further tightening tanker supply. The result has been a surge in key tanker rates to record highs. Rates to transport crude from the Middle East to Asia aboard a VLCC recently exceeded $1.2 million per day, up from roughly $30,000 a day in January, according to shipping broker Poten & Partners. As a result, freight costs that once accounted for around 3% of the delivered price of a barrel now represent roughly 27%. These costs are unlikely to normalise until trade flows return to something resembling their pre-war pattern. Indeed, a further recovery in exports through Hormuz may initially worsen the situation by increasing demand for the elaborate shuttle networks now required to move crude safely through the region. REFINING CRUNCH The loss of refining capacity in the Middle East and Russia, where Ukrainian drone attacks have crippled dozens of plants, has compounded the problem, particularly for diesel. Diesel prices have surged to record highs, becoming a [USN:L6N45E0T3 TEXT:"major political concern"] for U.S. President Donald Trump ahead of next month's midterm elections, as diesel powers much of modern industry, agriculture and manufacturing. The Group of Seven's decision last week to [USN:B5N44301Y TEXT:"release diesel"] from strategic stocks will likely provide only temporary relief as it does nothing to restore lost refining capacity. What’s more, refiners are increasingly competing for the medium-sour crude grades that generate higher diesel yields. Those barrels are concentrated in the Middle East and Russia, precisely the regions where supply disruptions remain most severe. That dynamic is creating a feedback loop. Tight refining capacity boosts diesel prices, which increases demand for diesel-rich crude grades, which in turn supports crude prices. The result is that oil prices are no longer primarily a function of supply, but of the industry's ability to transport and process crude – making it much more challenging to bring these prices down. item.title: India may be best placed to fill a China-sized hole in fuel exports
item.description: China's decision to suspend fuel exports for October has raised fresh fears of a further tightening in global markets.
item.dc:creator: Gavin Maguire
item.content:encoded: China's decision to suspend fuel exports for October has raised fresh fears of a further tightening in global markets. But a combination of rebounding crude oil imports and recent tax cuts on fuel exports makes India well-placed to fill the void. India has the world's [USN:L4N4070OR TEXT:"fourth-largest refinery system"], with 23 refineries capable of processing roughly 5.6 million barrels per day (bpd) of crude oil, Indian state data show. That refining footprint compares with more than 18 million bpd capacity in China and the US and roughly 6.7 million bpd of capacity in Russia, according to the Energy Institute, and traditionally makes India a key fuel supplier to a slew of Asian economies. India is also the consistently larger fuel exporter compared to China, with India's combined shipments of diesel, gasoline and jet fuel hitting roughly 47 million metric tons in 2025 compared with China's 25.4 million tons, data from Kpler showed. However, India's combined exports of diesel, gasoline and jet fuel over the first nine months of 2026 have contracted by roughly 23%, or nearly 8 million metric tons, from a year earlier. The US-Israeli war on Iran has triggered steep cuts to oil supplies from the Middle East since late February, while sparking fuel and oil rationing across most major economies - including India - for the past several months. The Indian government also raised duties on fuel exports in the wake of the Iran war, ensuring that the country's refiners were dissuaded from shipping too much fuel overseas while domestic supplies were at risk of depletion. But the outlook for India's fuel exports is starting to brighten following two consecutive [USN:FWN45M14K TEXT:"cuts to fuel-export taxes"], which boost the appeal of steering more fuel onto the export arena. CLIMBING CRUDE IMPORTS A [USN:L1N45R00B TEXT:"steep rebound in Middle Eastern crude oil exports"] is likely a major driver behind the easing of India's fuel-export taxes. India has traditionally sourced around 45% to 50% of its crude oil from the Middle East, with around 9.4 million metric tons of Middle Eastern oil arriving in India each month in 2025, Kpler data showed. But the war in Iran, which kicked off in late February, resulted in India's average oil imports from the Middle East dropping to less than 6 million tons a month from March through July. That in turn triggered a broader tightening in India's oil reserves and prompted stepped-up oil imports from other origins, which cost more and took longer to reach India's refineries. Oil flows from the Middle East have now started to recover, however, with deliveries to India in September topping 11.3 million tons, Kpler data showed. That is India's highest monthly oil haul from the Middle East since February and has restored confidence among Indian officials that fuel exports can start to be elevated again. KEY DESTINATIONS The top destinations for Indian fuel exports in 2025 were the United Arab Emirates, Australia, Tanzania, Singapore and South Africa, Kpler data showed. With tanker traffic through and around the Strait of Hormuz still impacted by the Iran conflict, Indian fuel exporters will presumably prioritize shipments to other markets which are not impacted by the war's fallout. Singapore and Australia are obvious candidates for stepped-up shipments from India over the near term, given their established track records of being regular and reliable buyers of Indian fuels. But with China expected to be out of the market for the next few weeks at least, Indian fuel sellers will likely also be able to target markets such as Indonesia, Vietnam and the Philippines, which used to be heavily reliant on China for much of their fuel inputs. If Indian refiners can successfully step up supplies to needy buyers just as China steps back from the export market, India could establish itself as one of the world's most important marginal suppliers of refined fuels. That role has traditionally belonged to China, whose vast refining system has long acted as a pressure valve for regional fuel markets. But Beijing's repeated willingness to curb exports in favour of domestic energy security means that fuel importers can no longer assume Chinese barrels will be available when shortages emerge. India is increasingly offering an alternative. Its refiners are highly export-oriented, its links with Middle Eastern crude suppliers are strengthening again and policymakers now appear more comfortable with allowing a greater share of fuel production to reach international markets. China's export suspension may prove temporary. The larger significance is that global fuel markets are being forced to identify who can step in when China steps back. With crude supplies recovering, export restrictions easing and spare refining capacity available, India looks better positioned than any other country to fill that role. For fuel consumers across Asia, that could make India more than just a major exporter. It could make India the new swing supplier that helps keep regional energy markets balanced during periods of disruption.
