item.title: US accuses California woman of spying for China, surveilling Taiwan president's son
item.description: US authorities arrested a California woman on Sunday and accused her of spying on a son of Taiwan's president at the behest of Chinese officials, the FBI said.
item.dc:creator: Kanishka Singh
item.content:encoded: US authorities arrested a California woman on Sunday and accused her of spying on a son of Taiwan's president at the behest of Chinese officials, the FBI said. The FBI arrested Wanying Zhang, also known as Heather, at Los Angeles International Airport on Sunday before her planned departure to China, the agency said in a statement. Authorities charged Zhang, 34, of Irvine, California, with acting as an unregistered foreign agent. Zhang surveilled a son of Taiwanese President Lai Ching-te, the FBI said. The agency did not directly name Zhang's alleged target, but later shared a New York Post report identifying him as Lai Ting-yu, a US resident. Taiwan's presidential office described Zhang's actions as a "typical case of transnational repression" and thanked the US government for protecting Taiwanese citizens. "Our country expresses the strongest condemnation of such barbaric conduct that disregards human rights and the sovereignty of nations," spokesperson Karen Kuo said in a statement. China's foreign ministry did not respond to a request for comment. Lai and his Democratic Progressive Party champion [USN:L1N45H067 TEXT:"Taiwan's separate identity"] from China , a position that frequently angers Beijing, which views the island as Chinese territory. Lai says only Taiwan's people can decide their future. The Justice Department said Zhang traveled to Seattle in 2025 at the direction of Chinese officials and sent them photos, video and license plate information of the Taiwanese president's son and his family. Zhang used tradecraft to avoid detection and never notified Washington that she was acting for a foreign government, Bill Essayli, the first assistant US attorney for the Central District of California, said in a statement. It was not immediately clear whether Zhang has a defense attorney. She will appear on Monday in a Los Angeles federal court, Essayli said. Washington [USN:L1N45N06U TEXT:"does not have formal diplomatic ties"] with Taiwan, but the United States is the island's most important international backer and weapons supplier.

item.title: Euro sinks to 17-month low as French fiscal woes spur contagion fears
item.description: The euro slid sharply on Monday to a 17-month low as fiscal worries in France in the wake of a steep bond market rout stoked contagion fears in the region, helping the dollar shrug off soft US jobs data that dented near-term rate hike expectations.
item.dc:creator: Ankur Banerjee
item.content:encoded: The euro slid sharply on Monday to a 17-month low as [USN:L6N45O0HP TEXT:"fiscal worries in France"] in the wake of a steep bond market rout stoked contagion fears in the region, helping the dollar shrug off [USN:L1N45N170 TEXT:"soft US jobs data"] that dented near-term rate hike expectations. The euro sank to as low as $1.1161 in Asian hours, its weakest level since May 2025, after four straight weekly declines, weighed down by France's debt levels and concerns about political gridlock ahead of next year's election. The single currency was last down 0.68% at $1.1176, while weakening 0.5% against the Swiss franc and sliding 0.39% against sterling . "Don't stand in front of the train," said Chris Weston, head of research at Pepperstone, warning against betting on a quick rebound. He said the move was a continuation of recent fiscal issues, with "possibly a whiff of contagion creeping in." Brent Donnelly, president of foreign exchange trading at analytics firm Spectra Markets, said the French politics trade that many expected would escalate this winter as April 2027 elections neared is here now. "It's not completely obvious what might fix things here as any budget promises made by the French government now are not super credible with a change of power coming soon," he said. The bond market ruction and the euro's weakness spurred concerns that France's troubles could spread across the euro zone similar to the debt crisis more than a decade ago and force the [USN:L1N45N0CH TEXT:"European Central Bank"] to help [USN:L8N45O0YO TEXT:"shore"] up French debt. Some analysts though said it was still too early to judge whether there was growing risk of contagion. Ninghui Liu, head of investment strategy and research for APAC at State Street Investment Management, said France's fiscal position was becoming increasingly unstable but noted that the market had only been reacting since last week. "For now, I think it's more of a country story rather than the euro crisis," he added. Should the strain deepen, other euro zone members would not stand aside, Liu said. "Germany definitely will step in, because they are the ones who want to make sure that the EU can still hold." BOND ROUT HANGOVER Markets are also still reeling from the recent bond rout, which drove global borrowing costs to multi-decade highs and pummelled French debt as investors fretted over inflation risks from soaring oil prices. French bond futures dipped 0.22%, close to record lows they have been hugging in recent days, while German Bund futures rose 0.1%, highlighting the divergence in bond markets as investors seek shelter in relatively safer debt. The premium of French 10-year borrowing costs over Germany's ended last week at 140 basis points, after gaining 34 bps, its biggest weekly jump in 17 years, according to LSEG data. . The yield on US 10-year Treasury notes was 1.6 bps lower at 5.260%, as some calm returned following a spike to a 24-year high last week that rattled markets. Sterling slipped 0.25% to $1.3205, while the Japanese yen changed hands at 157.92 per dollar. That left the dollar index , which measures the US currency against six major units, up 0.47% at 102.37. "The dollar is the main winner in the current environment as not only is the rise in Treasury yields boosting the appeal of US assets, but the broad selloff in debt globally is fuelling safe-haven flows into the greenback," said Matthew Ryan, head of market strategy at Ebury. Apart from the euro's troubles, much of the dollar strength in recent weeks has come from traders pricing in Fed rate hikes in the coming months. However, data on Friday showed US job growth slowed more than expected in September, denting those expectations. Traders are now pricing in a 78% chance of the US central bank holding rates steady in October, compared with 36% a week earlier, the CME FedWatch tool showed. They still expect a hike in December and another two in the first half of 2027.

item.title: Euro pummelled by France's debt burden; stocks mixed
item.description: Asian stocks made brisk gains on Monday as investors pared back expectations of a Federal Reserve rate hike this month, while the euro sank to a 17-month low on concerns over France's deteriorating fiscal position.
item.dc:creator: Rae Wee
item.content:encoded: Asian stocks made brisk gains on Monday as investors pared back expectations of a Federal Reserve rate hike this month, while the euro sank to a 17-month low on concerns over France's deteriorating fiscal position. The euro tumbled more than 0.8% to $1.1161 in Asia, before paring some of those losses to trade at $1.1178. The common currency, which lost roughly 2.5% last month, has come under pressure due to [USN:L6N45O0HP TEXT:"mounting worries"] about high debt levels and political gridlock in France ahead of next year's presidential election. The premium investors demand to hold French 10-year bonds over safer Germany [USN:L8N45O0YO TEXT:"shot above 150 basis points"] on Friday, stoking concerns of a broader spillover across European markets. "We're starting to see some cracks in overall euro sentiment," said Bart Wakabayashi, branch manager at State Street in Tokyo, as a generally positive mood on the euro zone and an outlook for rate hikes have quickly darkened. "Real money are selling euro against the dollar very aggressively," he said. French OAT futures were down 0.23%, while German bund futures edged up 0.1%. The euro's slide gave the dollar an extra lift, adding to support from elevated US Treasury yields and pushing the greenback up 0.5% against a basket of currencies to 102.39. . Sterling slipped 0.23% to $1.3207, while the yen fell 0.15% to 158.10 per dollar. "Tighter policy elsewhere and a growing case for an October Fed pause are US dollar headwinds. But US growth outperformance and strong foreign appetite for US securities keep US dollar risks skewed to the upside," said Elias Haddad, global head of markets strategy at BBH. Bonds, meanwhile, held steady, with benchmark 10-year US Treasury yields retreating slightly to 5.2686% while two-year yields stood at 4.8101%. Still, yields across major economies remain near multi-year highs as bond prices come under pressure from deteriorating government finances, a glut of issuance and elevated energy costs. A trader, who declined to be identified as they were not authorised to speak to the media, said clients have expressed reluctance to buy US Treasuries unless there was a "material improvement" in the Middle East war. OCTOBER FED HIKE OFF THE TABLE Trading was thin in Asia with holidays in China, South Korea and Australia's New South Wales, though equity markets took their cue from [USN:L6N45O132 TEXT:"Wall Street's moves"] on Friday. Data last week showed US job growth [USN:L1N45N170 TEXT:"slowed more than expected"] in September and the nonfarm payrolls count for the prior two months was revised sharply lower, which investors believed would almost take another rate hike from the Fed this month off the table. That helped Japan's Nikkei (.N225) rise 2%, while MSCI's broadest index of Asia-Pacific shares outside Japan (.MISX00000PUS) advanced 0.9%. Nasdaq futures were flat while S&P 500 futures eased 0.1%. EUROSTOXX 50 futures and DAX futures inched down, though FTSE futures tacked on 0.26%. "Labour conditions are stable overall, but Friday's downward revisions signal that the US economy has lost jobs in two out of the nine months year to date, and the risk of further employment losses means that the Fed can't hike another 100 basis points from here, which is what the curve is pricing in," said Jose Torres, senior economist at Interactive Brokers. Investors are now pricing in less than a 20% chance that the Fed could raise rates this month, as compared to a 64% chance a week ago, according to the CME FedWatch tool. But traders still expect a hike in December. In Brazil, markets are expected to jump later in the day after it became clear that Brazilian Senator Flavio Bolsonaro [USN:L6N45Q04L TEXT:"will face"] President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva in the runoff of a presidential election, doing better than expected in the first round of voting. Elsewhere, oil prices [USN:L1N45Q068 TEXT:"edged lower"] as rising Middle East crude exports and a release of oil stocks by the Group of Seven nations boosted supplies, offsetting concerns about further damage to Gulf oil infrastructure amid the US-Israeli war on Iran. Brent crude futures were down 0.5% at $101.75 per barrel while US crude slid 0.9% to $90.29 a barrel. [O/R} Spot gold fell 0.24% to $4,132.33 an ounce.

item.title: Lula admite surpresa com resultado de votação, mas diz que 2º turno será nova campanha
item.description: A derrota inesperada no primeiro turno para Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) por dois pontos percentuais foi uma ducha de água fria na campanha do presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT), mas o próprio candidato à reeleição tentou injetar ânimo em seus apoiadores ao prometer que começará de imediato uma nova campanha para virar o resultado na votação decisiva em 25 de outubro.
item.dc:creator: Lisandra Paraguassu
item.content:encoded: A derrota inesperada no primeiro turno para Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) por dois pontos percentuais foi uma ducha de água fria na campanha do presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT), mas o próprio candidato à reeleição tentou injetar ânimo em seus apoiadores ao prometer que começará de imediato uma nova campanha para virar o resultado na votação decisiva em 25 de outubro. "O resultado muitas vezes é inesperado, a gente nunca consegue tudo aquilo que a gente queria. Eu confesso para vocês que eu estava convencido que ia ganhar as eleições no primeiro turno", disse Lula em pronunciamento após a votação deste domingo. "Mas a gente tem o segundo turno e o segundo turno é a hora da prova dos nove". A apuração do primeiro turno neste domingo terminou com Flávio com 47,03% dos votos válidos contra 45,16% de Lula, uma diferença de 2,2 milhões de votos. O resultado contrariou quase todas as pesquisas de intenção de votos para o primeiro turno, que apontavam uma liderança de Lula. O presidente, que votou em São Paulo, embarcará de volta para Brasília na manhã de segunda-feira e prometeu retomar a campanha a partir de terça. Já na segunda-feira a coordenação de campanha irá se reunir para discutir os próximos passos, segundo o presidente do PT, Edinho Silva. "A partir de amanhã a gente começa uma nova campanha, uma campanha apenas entre dois candidatos em que a gente vai mostrar a diferença entre as propostas que existem para o Brasil", disse Lula. Fontes da campanha admitem que o caminho não será fácil. Nunca um candidato que ficou atrás no primeiro turno conseguiu reverter o resultado para o segundo. Mas, segundo uma das fontes, são "apenas 2 milhões" de votos, enquanto mais de 33 milhões de eleitores se abstiveram de votar. "Temos que chamar essas pessoas para votar no segundo turno", disse a fonte. Em seu discurso, Lula estava acompanhado de sua equipe e de diversos candidatos aliados derrotados a vários postos, como os ex-ministros Fernando Haddad, Simone Tebet e Marina Silva. O abatimento era visível no grupo, mas Lula tentou animar seus apoiadores, após ser recebido sob os tradicionais gritos de "Olê, Olê, Olá, Lula". "Eu sou muito bom de mata-mata. O jogo vai começar, estamos na prorrogação e vamos convencer o povo brasileiro de continuarmos um projeto de desenvolvimento", disse.

item.title: Flávio diz que resultado do 1º turno da eleição decreta "fim da era do PT"
item.description: Em discurso após terminar na liderança o primeiro turno da eleição presidencial neste domingo, o senador Flávio Bolsonaro (PL-RJ) afirmou que o resultado das urnas decreta "o fim da era PT" e comprometeu-se com o fim da reeleição caso eleito, afirmando que só precisará de um mandato para resolver os problemas do país.
item.dc:creator: Ricardo Brito
item.content:encoded: Em discurso após terminar na liderança o primeiro turno da eleição presidencial neste domingo, o senador Flávio Bolsonaro (PL-RJ) afirmou que o resultado das urnas decreta "o fim da era PT" e comprometeu-se com o fim da reeleição caso eleito, afirmando que só precisará de um mandato para resolver os problemas do país. Em um breve e tumultuado pronunciamento a jornalistas na porta do comitê de sua campanha em Brasília, o senador disse que espera que após o segundo turno de 25 de outubro o Brasil "mande um recado" que quer um governo mais moderno e com menos ministérios. "É o fim da era do PT. Está decretado o fim da era do PT, é a mudança no nosso país", disse ele. "Estou muito feliz com a possibilidade real de, daqui a três semanas, o Brasil dar uma resposta de que quer um governo mais moderno, com menos ministérios", acrescentou. O senador afirmou precisar de apenas um mandato para cuidar dos problemas do Brasil. "Eu sou o único candidato que assumiu um compromisso pelo fim da reeleição, porque eu só preciso de um mandato para colocar o brasileiro e a brasileira no centro do meu governo, para que eu possa atacar e resolver os problemas reais do Brasil." O senador também disse que pretende "resgatar a democracia" e indicar ministros do Supremo Tribunal Federal (STF) que não vão "interferir em eleições". As críticas ao STF se tornaram uma das principais pautas de Flávio e impulsionaram a forte bancada de senadores aliados eleitos neste domingo. FUNK, CHURRASCO E O PAI A Reuters assistiu a vídeos filmados de dentro do QG da campanha durante a apuração dos votos neste domingo em que Flávio aparece dançando funk com a esposa Fernanda e aliados, como o coordenador de campanha, senador Rogério Marinho (PL-RN), e o candidato a vice-presidente, deputado Alfredo Gaspar (PL-AL), além da economista Daniella Marques, cotada para ocupar um cargo de relevo no próximo governo e conselheira da pauta econômica. Aos aliados, Flávio agradeceu o empenho de todos e disse ter certeza que estará comemorando após o segundo turno a liberdade do país e o fim da era do PT. "Eu me sinto muito preparado para ser presidente da República hoje", disse ele, sob aplausos. O senador afirmou que vai fazer um governo inspirado no pai, o ex-presidente Jair Bolsonaro, que está preso cumprindo pena após ter sido condenado por tentativa de golpe de Estado, mas ressaltou que será "ainda melhor do que o dele". "Aqui do nosso lado temos várias pessoas que fizeram parte do governo dele, e ainda há mais pessoas que podem somar a este time. O jeito que a gente está chegando é muito libertador, no peito e na raça, com um time que é o melhor time que já vi disputando uma campanha presidencial", afirmou. O candidato do PL afirmou que a partir de segunda-feira vai começar do zero, porque o segundo turno é uma outra eleição. "Vou descansar minha voz para a partir de amanhã continuar a voz no máximo, pulmão no máximo, energia no máximo, esperança no máximo e certeza da vitória no máximo", ressaltou. Olhando para um mapa de votação sobre a votação no Nordeste, o presidenciável disse que quer uma oportunidade para mostrar para a parte em vermelho -- numa referência aos eleitores de Lula -- que "a gente é fundamentalmente melhor que o PT". "Eles estão escravizados e nós vamos libertar", disse. "Se comparar com a eleição passada, no Nordeste a gente tirou muita diferença, foram quase 20 pontos no Nordeste... há fadiga de material do lado de lá e nosso projeto está mostrando que somos muito melhor do que eles", acrescentou.

item.title: India seen kicking off rate hike cycle as inflation broadens, peers turn hawkish
item.description: Investors have loaded up on bets that the Reserve Bank of India will raise rates this week, warning that it risks falling behind the curve as inflation quickens, growth remains resilient and major central banks turn more hawkish.
item.dc:creator: Jaspreet Kalra
item.content:encoded: Investors have loaded up on bets that the Reserve Bank of India will raise rates this week, warning that it risks falling behind the curve as inflation quickens, growth remains resilient and major central banks turn more hawkish. Nearly 60% of economists [USN:L4N45K09D TEXT:"polled"] by Reuters, 35 out of 61, expect a 25-basis-point rate hike at its policy meeting on Wednesday. Market pricing is more decisive with swap markets fully pricing in an increase in borrowing costs. If delivered, the hike would be the RBI's first in nearly four years and lift the benchmark repo rate (INREPO=ECI) from 5.25% where it has remained for nearly 10 months. The Monetary Policy Committee cut rates by a cumulative 125 bps in 2025 from 6.5% to 5.25%. "We now sense that the RBI has little reason to wait, given visibility of growth remains high, inflation appears to be broadening, and the need to wait for clarity on the global front declines," said Rahul Bajoria, India and ASEAN economist at BofA Global Research. Bajoria expects the central bank to kick off a 100-basis-point tightening cycle in October with subsequent hikes penciled in for December and the first half of 2027. "This essentially is no longer just about reversing the incremental cut that the RBI had delivered last December but actually taking away the monetary punchbowl before inflation risks become entrenched," he said. With inflation running above the RBI's target and markets already pricing in higher borrowing costs, the central bank's decision and guidance are likely to shape expectations for the path of interest rates and capital flows. A benign inflation backdrop early in the year had given the RBI room to wait even as the Iran war sparked a surge in oil prices, but inflationary [USN:L6N45K0J1 TEXT:"pressures have since broadened"] beyond food and fuel. Consumer inflation picked up in August to 4.82%, above the RBI's 4% medium-term target for a third consecutive month, with prices across nearly half of the CPI basket rising at or above the target. The economy grew 7.8% in the April-June quarter. HOLD MAY DRAW PUSHBACK Several major central banks, including the US Federal Reserve and Bank of Japan, have raised rates since the US-Israeli war on Iran began seven months ago. Traders and analysts now expect the RBI to follow suit, warning that a pushback may be in store if rates are maintained. "A hold will not be taken positively by the currency market and even the long end of the bond market may face some pressure," said Vivek Rajpal, Asia macro strategist at JB Drax Honore, adding that the RBI will also need to signal openness to raising rates further if needed. The rupee remains [USN:L4N45M0LB TEXT:"under pressure"] and is about 1% off record lows hit in May. "India needs to act on multiple fronts and going to a neutral rate is part of the solution," he added, pointing to how inflation-adjusted interest rates in India remain quite low at a time when price pressures have deepened and global competition for capital has intensified. Higher rates could also make Indian bonds more attractive to foreign investors at a time when domestic stocks continue to struggle without clear AI opportunities. HIKE, BUT HOW MUCH? Economists at Nomura and Barclays have penciled in a shallow hike cycle of 25-50 bps while ANZ, BofA and Goldman Sachs anticipate between 75 and 100 bps of rate increases. Swap markets are pricing about 100 bps worth of hikes over the next 12 months and about 140 bps over the next 24 months. BofA's Bajoria reckons the RBI may not want to commit to a longer hiking cycle in October itself, but could be open to doing so in December. That would put the focus on any changes to the RBI's inflation and growth forecasts, as well as whether it changes its "neutral" policy stance, for clues on how far policymakers are prepared to take the tightening cycle. Goldman Sachs economists expect the stance could shift to "calibrated tightening" or "withdrawal of accommodation."

item.title: Georgia block party shooting kills two, injures dozens
item.description: A shooting early on Sunday at a Georgia block party left two people dead and almost three dozen injured, some critically, local and state officials said.
item.dc:creator: Svea Herbst-Bayliss
item.content:encoded: A shooting early on Sunday at a Georgia block party left two people dead and almost three dozen injured, some critically, local and state officials said. Dooly County Sheriff Craig Peavy told a news conference that two men, aged 21 and 23, were shot dead in Vienna, Georgia, about 135 miles (216 km) south of Atlanta. Thirty-five people were injured, mostly by gunshot wounds, officials told reporters. They said hundreds of people had attended the event, which came at the end of Dooly County High School's homecoming week. Authorities do not believe there is a remaining threat to the public, but have not publicly named any suspects or persons of interest, and have not identified a motive for the shooting. "We don't want to presume as to what caused it," said Chris Hosey, director of the Georgia Bureau of Investigation. Those wounded range in age from 14 to 51, officials said.

item.title: Saudi Arabia unexpectedly cuts November oil prices to Asia to 6-year lows
item.description: Saudi Arabia unexpectedly cut its oil prices for sale to Asia in November to six-year lows while raising them for northwest Europe and the Mediterranean, a pricing document showed on Monday.
item.dc:creator: Yomna Ehab, Siyi Liu
item.content:encoded: Saudi Arabia unexpectedly cut its oil prices for sale to Asia in November to six-year lows while raising them for northwest Europe and the Mediterranean, a pricing document showed on Monday. The largest Middle Eastern crude exporter set the November Arab Light crude oil official selling price to Asia at $5 a barrel below the average of Oman and Dubai prices, down $3 [USN:L1N44V0N1 TEXT:"from the previous month"]. The discount for November is the widest since June 2020, Reuters data showed. This was against expectations of a hike of up to $5 a barrel for the November OSP in a [USN:L4N45K0F8 TEXT:"Reuters survey"], in line with gains seen in the Middle Eastern benchmarks. State oil company Saudi Aramco (2222.SE) cut the November OSPs of heavier grades, Arab Medium and Arab Heavy, sold to Asia by $5 a barrel. Aramco has been looking at offering [USN:L4N45K0Q6 TEXT:"discounts"] for oil loaded off Oman to compensate buyers for record freight rates, people familiar with the matter said last week, as it sought to protect its market share after disruptions from the US-Israeli war against Iran affected exports. The OSP cuts appeared to be aimed at compensating buyers for the elevated freight costs, said three Asian refining sources who spoke on condition of anonymity. The cost of booking a very large crude carrier capable of hauling 2 million barrels of oil from the Gulf to China on a time charter basis was $1.2 million a day on Friday, according to LSEG data. It was about $80,000 a day a year ago. One of the sources also said the lower OSPs could offset the waiting time and longer voyage for Saudi oil exported from the Egyptian port of Sidi Kerir, where cargo loadings have been delayed. Since September, Saudi Aramco has sold millions of barrels of crude through ship-to-ship transfers outside the Strait of Hormuz, pushing oil flows through the strategic waterway to pre-conflict levels. The kingdom also [USN:L6N45L0WE TEXT:"resumed loading at the port of Yanbu"] on the Red Sea after a brief suspension as a drone attack shut its key East-West oil pipeline. Separately, Saudi Aramco raised the November OSPs for northwest Europe by $3 a barrel across all grades. Aramco kept prices unchanged for buyers in the United States.
